headline: Netanyahu offers to rotate Israeli premiership with main rival Eisenkot

paragraphs.text: Israel’s caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Saturday proposed a rotating premiership with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, who would go first, with the latter expected to announce the formation of a new government within days.

Proposing a unity government in a social media post, Netanyahu said “my responsibility as a leader requires me to set everything aside ... and agree that Gadi Eisenkot will serve first as prime minister, while I will serve as alternate prime minister at the beginning of the term”.
The offer came one day after Eisenkot vowed to announce the formation of Israel’s next government by the official deadline of 6 December, without using the option of a 14-day extension.
He is expected to form a coalition with anti-Netanyahu parties, but his centrist Yashar party has also been conducting negotiations with Netanyahu’s rightwing Likud.
On Friday, however, Eisenkot accused Likud of stalling coalition talks in an effort to bring about new elections.
“Likud ... has been unwilling to compromise and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table,” Eisenkot said in a statement.
His wide-ranging camp has faced divisions over whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties, the Arab-majority lists, or form a unity government with Likud.
Netanyahu opponents scoffed at his offer of a rotating premiership.

Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Arab-majority Joint List, which is expected to support an Eisenkot-led government without joining it, wrote: “The democratic majority has decided: this bloodstained, neglectful government must go. It is time to fulfill the shared will of the entire public, Jews and Arabs alike, and remove Netanyahu this (upcoming) week.”

Former premier Yair Lapid, who co-chairs the centrist Beyachad (Together) party, wrote: “Netanyahu’s proposal is yet another transparent con by a serial fraudster who has deceived every partner and violated every agreement.”
Eisenkot’s Yashar party has so far agreed coalition deals with the left-leaning Democrats and the rightwing Yisrael Beiteinu party.
Together, they have a combined total of 36 lawmakers – far short of the 61 needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.

Israeli media reported that Mansour Abbas, the leader of the Arab-Israeli party Ra’am, is expected on Saturday to recognise Hamas as a “terror group” – a move that could pave the way for his party to join a possible Eisenkot-led coalition.
But some of Eisenkot’s allies have voiced opposition to relying on the support of the Arab-majority lists, which made unprecedented gains in the election.
Meanwhile, Britain, France and six other countries on Saturday issued a joint statement calling for postponed Palestinian legislative elections to take place in the first three months of 2027.

The vote was “essential” for a “democratic renewal” in the Palestinian territories and “is inseparable from the preservation of the two-state solution, which we remain steadfastly committed to”, they said.
The other countries behind the joint statement were Canada, Australia, Belgium, Luxembourg, Norway and Poland.
Last month, the Palestinian president, Mahmoud Abbas, postponed legislative elections to September next year.
The first legislative elections since 2006, which the international community has strongly advocated for, had been scheduled for 28 November, with a presidential election expected in early 2027.
“Twenty years after the last national election in Palestine”, Palestinians were still being denied “the right to express themselves democratically through the ballot box”, the eight countries said.
“The holding of free and transparent elections is essential to preserve the democratic principles that must remain at the heart of Palestinian institutions.”
The ministers also warned that their continued support for the Palestinian Authority went hand in hand with commitments on reform and democratic renewal.
Abbas’s office in October blamed the delay on “obstacles imposed by Israeli measures ... as well as the need to create appropriate political, security and on-the-ground conditions”.
Israel, which held its own elections late last month, rejected any responsibility for the delay.
